title: Biologists are using AI to track individual birds by their songs alone
summary: A paper published this month in Nature Methods relied on sound recordings and artificial intelligence to identify individual birds based on their songs alone.

image.caption: An ovenbird perched on a twig. The species has a rare trait with males sticking to one primary mating call through the course of their lives. (Nick Parayko)

blocks.text: Edmonton
A paper published this month in Nature Methods relied on sound recordings and artificial intelligence to identify individual birds based on their songs alone.
The male ovenbird is a one-hit wonder with a distinct mating call
From tweets to trills, birdsong can be as diverse as a symphony.
But ovenbirds — rotund, ground-dwelling warblers — have a strictly limited repertoire.
The male has a single song: a rapid melody often described as teacher-teacher-teacher.
To most ears, all ovenbirds sound the same, but each has its own, distinct take.
Now, biologists are using AI to help track the health of ovenbird populations by their signature songs alone.
Research published this month in the science journal Nature Methods relied on AI to identify individual ovenbirds in recordings gathered in Alberta and Pennsylvania.
One-track mind
The ovenbird’s “particular” setlist made it the ideal species to study, said lead researcher Sam Lapp, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Colorado.
“They are really pretty loyal to singing one very specific song,” said Lapp in an interview with CBC News.
“There are a lot of birds that do kind of crystallize a vocal signature over the course of their life. Often, that will incorporate several different songs into what we call a repertoire of the bird.
“But the ovenbird has this nice property of not only having one very stable song over time, but only singing one version of it.”

blocks.text: Ovenbirds sing their primary song in the spring, to defend their territory and attract a mate. And it remains a constant refrain throughout their lives.

Led by Lapp during his time with the Department of Biological Sciences at the University of Pittsburgh, the research team used recordings collected from nearly 130 sites in Pennsylvania over four years.
They trained an AI model to extract features that made songs unique and cluster similar ones together, assuming each bird would return to the same patch of forest every spring.

The team processed 9,072 hours of audio to track 405 individual birds. The researchers then tested the model against another set of recordings, collected throughout the mixed wood and boreal forests of Alberta during the 2016 spring breeding season.
Lapp said the model could link songs to individual birds with up to 96-per-cent accuracy.
It’s much less labour-intensive than leg banding, where biologists capture birds, carefully place markers around their ankles and then aim to catch them again the following spring.
He said the idea for the research came from a collaboration with Alberta biologists who were attempting to pinpoint the location of birds across vast distances using a grid of microphones.
'Kind of wondrous'
Human ears cannot distinguish individual ovenbirds in real time because their vocal nuances happen too quickly, Lapp said.
But on spectrographs — visual representations of sound — each bird’s distinctive song comes into focus, Lapp said.
“I started thinking, if my eyes can see these patterns, can we teach a machine to be able to recognize these patterns and do an automated version of individual recognition?

“Even if you're obsessed with birds and really into identifying species, it's so surprising and exciting and it's kind of wondrous that this level of information exists that we’ve just been missing ... but is there if you're listening closely enough.”

blocks.text: Erin Bayne, University of Alberta biology professor and a co-author of the study, has been keeping an ear on ovenbirds for years and knows the rigours of annual population monitoring.
During his PhD, Bayne spent tens of thousands of hours tracking banded birds, to the point where he could tell individuals apart by their unique vocal variations.
“What that guy is saying over there is a little different from that guy over there,” he said. “I knew who was who.
“And they're incredibly polite when they sing. It's quite funny actually. One bird will sing and then the other one will wait until he finishes, but then instantaneously will sing after that.”
Birds of a feather talk together
Bayne said the study shows that avian communication is far more complex than most people assume, and that conversations are happening, even if we don’t understand the language.
Just like humans have distinct speech patterns, biologists are learning how certain animals also develop a voice of their own, Bayne said.

“In many ways, it's not surprising that individual birds or individual animals have something different that's detectable. I think the more we look into it, the more it's going to be quite simple to see that it's true.”
While the model has limitations, the study researchers hope it provides a less invasive way to understand the health of songbirds, merely by listening in.
The AI system cannot accurately track the varied calls of female ovenbirds or the simple vocalizations made by juveniles.
The current program would also fall short for monitoring species such as magpies and mockingbirds that constantly mimic new sounds or sing dozens of different songs.
It would work best for birds that sing one, unchanging song throughout their lives — roughly 30 per cent of songbird species — as well as certain species of bats and owls.
The researchers put the program code on open-source sites, to help other biologists track the survival of other songbird populations or even other species.

blocks.text: Richard Hedley, a statistical ecologist with the Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute who was not involved in the research, said it has incredible potential.
While AI acoustic monitoring has been used to track birds at the species level for years, showing that it can distinguish between individual birds is an impressive feat, he said.
There is a wealth of existing acoustic recordings that could be harnessed in new ways, he said.
“It can take many hours just to catch a single bird. So the idea that we can just do this by putting a microphone on the bird's territory is really promising.”
